```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

The framework does not fix the target model. This page covers the two targets beyond the Cox model:
the grouped-time model of an outcome recorded in intervals, and a neural-network risk score. Both enter
the same objective, $-\ell(\theta) + \eta\,\mathcal{B}_G(\theta)$, through `cv.bregsurv()`.

## The grouped-time model

Subject $i$ is at risk in intervals $1, \dots, t_i$; the event, if any, happens in interval $t_i$. The
hazard of interval $k$ is

$$
h_{ik} = g^{-1}\!\left(\gamma_{s(i)k} + \mathbf z_i^\top \boldsymbol\beta\right),
$$

with one baseline parameter $\gamma_{sk}$ per stratum and interval and the complementary log-log link
(`link = "cloglog"`, the grouped proportional-hazards model, whose $\boldsymbol\beta$ has the meaning
of a Cox model's) or the logit link. The log-likelihood is a Bernoulli likelihood over the
person-intervals at risk.

```{r}
tg <- target_discrete(interval = week, event = died, z = x, stratum = center)
```

An interval in which no training subject has the event has a maximum-likelihood hazard of zero; its
baseline parameter is held at a floor corresponding to a hazard of $10^{-8}$ instead of diverging.

### The three members on a discrete target

**Kullback--Leibler: absolute risk.** The divergence is taken between the external and target hazards
of every interval at risk. It reduces to the Bernoulli likelihood with each outcome replaced by a soft
target, $(y_{ik} + \eta\,\tilde h_{ik})/(1+\eta)$, exactly as the Cox member replaces each event
indicator. It needs the external model's interval hazards $\tilde h_{ik}$, which a Cox model gives
together with its baseline hazard:

```{r}
# a registry Cox model: coefficients plus baseline cumulative-hazard increments over your K intervals
rl <- release_model(beta = beta_registry, baseline = dH0)
# or the interval hazards themselves, one row per subject
rl <- release_model(hazard = H_registry)
fit_kl <- cv.bregsurv(tg, rl, member = "kl")
```

A coefficient vector alone says nothing about interval hazards, so `release_coef()` cannot inform this
member on a discrete target.

**Mahalanobis.** Under the complementary log-log link the coefficients compare directly with a Cox
model's, so a released coefficient vector (with its precision matrix, if any) enters as for a Cox target:

```{r}
fit_m <- cv.bregsurv(tg, release_coef(beta_registry, Q), member = "mahalanobis")
```

**Composite likelihood.** External records on the same intervals enter with weight $\eta$ and their own
baseline parameters:

```{r}
rec <- release_records(z_ext, interval = week_ext, event = died_ext)
fit_c <- cv.bregsurv(tg, rec)
```

Every member accepts `penalty = "ridge"`, `"lasso"` or `"enet"`. Fits use Fisher scoring with the
baseline parameters profiled out, and proximal Newton with coordinate descent under an $\ell_1$ penalty.
The objective is scaled per subject, as for the Cox estimators, so $\eta$ has the same meaning on both
targets.

### Choosing the weight

Every discrete member, linear or neural, is scored by the same criterion: the held-out negative
log-likelihood per subject of the grouped-time model, pooled over the folds. With the same `seed`, all of
them share one partition, so their `value`s compare directly.

```{r}
own <- cv.bregsurv(tg)
c(target_only = own$value, kl = fit_kl$value, mahalanobis = fit_m$value)
predict(fit_kl, newz = x_new, stratum = center_new, type = "survival")
```

The Kullback--Leibler member on the grouped-time model is the method of @wang2025discretekl; with
$\eta = 0$ every member reduces to the target-only grouped-time model.

## Neural-network risk scores

`score = nn_score()` replaces $\mathbf z^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ by a feed-forward network. Only the
Kullback--Leibler member is defined for it, since the other two compare coefficients.

* On a **discrete target** the network outputs one logit per interval, a logistic-hazard model, trained
  on the soft targets above: the external model is distilled into the network, and $\eta = 0$ is the
  network trained on your data alone.
* On a **Cox target** the network outputs a risk score, trained on the partial likelihood with each event
  indicator blended with the external pseudo-event weight. It is scored by the same cross-validated
  partial-likelihood loss as the linear Cox members, on the same folds, so a network and a linear model
  can be compared.

```{r}
install.packages("torch"); torch::install_torch()   # once

spec <- nn_score(hidden = c(128, 128, 128, 128), dropout = 0.1)
tg_nn <- target_discrete(interval = week, event = died, z = x, score = spec)
net <- cv.bregsurv(tg_nn, release_model(beta = beta_registry, baseline = dH0))
net$eta; net$path
```

The training protocol: within each fold, an event-stratified 20% of the training part is held out for
early stopping, the covariates are standardized on the rest, and every candidate starts from the same
initialization. The learning rate is chosen first, at $\eta = 0$, then $\eta$; the final network is
trained on all the data for the median best epoch of the selected setting. The default network has four
residual blocks of width 128, each a linear layer, layer normalization, ReLU and dropout.

Networks are random even with a seed fixed, across platforms and versions of `torch`; on one machine and
one version, a fixed `seed` reproduces the fit.
